w: Opened in 1911, the Grundy is a Grade II listed Edwardian building still owned and run by Blackpool Council. Its programme swings from regional historic works through to recent contemporary art, and its listing was shared with the adjoining Central Library, both designated on the same day in October 1983.
s: Grade II Edwardian gallery, historic to contemporary art
_facts: Owned and operated by Blackpool Council
Listed alongside adjoining Central Library on 20 October 1983

w: Opened on 14 May 1894 and modelled on the Eiffel Tower, Blackpool Tower rose to 518 feet, briefly the tallest man-made structure in the British Empire. The wider Tower Buildings - a three-storey red-brick block holding the tower itself, a circus, the Tower Ballroom and roof gardens - were Grade I listed in 1973.
s: 1894 tower modelled on the Eiffel, once Empire's tallest
_facts: Tower Buildings complex Grade I listed in 1973

w: Blackpool Zoo covers 32 acres (13 hectares) on the edge of the resort and is owned by the Spanish leisure group Parques Reunidos. It cares for more than 1,000 animals drawn from every corner of the globe, one of the larger wildlife collections on this stretch of the Lancashire coast.

Marsh Mill is an 18th-century tower windmill raised in 1794 by Ralph Slater for the local landowner Bold Hesketh. It ground corn in Thornton, just inland from Blackpool, until the 1920s, and has since been fully restored - a rare complete example of an English windmill, and Grade II* listed.
s: 1794 tower windmill, restored, Grade II* listed
_facts: Worked as a corn mill until the 1920s

w: Little Marton Mill is a 19th-century tower windmill built in 1838 by John Hays to grind corn in Marton, on Blackpool's landward edge. It worked until 1928 and still stands today, a Grade II listed reminder of the farmland this stretch of the resort was built over.

n: Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes, Blackpool
w: On Whinney Heys Road stands the Shrine of Our Lady of Lourdes, known locally simply as 'The Shrine' - or, more wryly, the 'Bishop's folly'. Grade II* listed and now in the care of the Historic Chapels Trust, it is easily confused with the unrelated 'White Church' over in nearby Ansdell.
s: Grade II* shrine locally nicknamed the 'Bishop's folly'
_facts: Located on Whinney Heys Road, Blackpool
Owned by the Historic Chapels Trust

w: Central Pier is one of Blackpool's three piers, opened in 1868 as the resort's Victorian tourist boom took off. True to its name, it holds the middle ground of the trio strung along the seafront, each one built within a few decades of the others to give day-trippers somewhere to walk out over the sand.
s: Middle of Blackpool's three Victorian piers, built 1868

w: Blackpool Grand Theatre is known locally simply as The Grand. Since 2006 it has also held the title National Theatre of Variety, and the building is Grade II* listed, one of the seaside resort's surviving grand Victorian and Edwardian playhouses in the heart of the town centre.
s: 'The Grand': National Theatre of Variety since 2006
_facts: Also titled National Theatre of Variety since 2006

w: The Opera House sits inside Blackpool's Winter Gardens complex, first opened in 1889 and rebuilt twice, in 1910 and 1939. Grade II* listed like the rest of the Gardens, it seats 2,812 across three levels - the third largest theatre in the UK after London's Hammersmith Apollo and the Edinburgh Playhouse.
s: 2,812-seat theatre, third largest in the UK
_facts: Part of the Winter Gardens, Grade II* listed
Third largest theatre in the UK after Hammersmith Apollo and Edinburgh Playhouse

w: Opened in 1878, the Winter Gardens combines a theatre, ballroom and conference halls under one Grade II* listed roof. Every British Prime Minister since WWII has reportedly addressed an audience here, and the venue has hosted the Blackpool Dance Festival since 1920 and the World Matchplay darts since 1994.
s: 1878 complex: every postwar PM, darts since 1994
_facts: Hosts party conferences and the TUC
Blackpool Dance Festival since 1920, World Matchplay darts since 1994

w: Stanley Park, Blackpool's 104-hectare primary park, was laid out in the 1920s by landscape architect Thomas Mawson. Its Italian gardens hold a marble fountain and Medici Lions, overlooked by an Art Deco cafe; beyond lie a boating lake, a bandstand and a golf course by Alister MacKenzie. Grade II* listed.
s: 1920s Grade II* park with Medici Lions and a model village
_facts: 104 hectares, laid out 1920s by Thomas Mawson
Grade II* listed, Register of Historic Parks and Gardens
Italian gardens with marble fountain and Medici Lions
Golf course designed by Alister MacKenzie
